stimulus.text:
Black population of the United States, counted by the federal census:

| Year | Enslaved people | Free Black people |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1790 | 697,681 | 59,527 |
| 1800 | 893,602 | 108,435 |
| 1820 | 1,538,022 | 233,634 |
| 1840 | 2,487,355 | 386,293 |

Congress banned the importation of enslaved people from abroad, effective January 1, 1808.
stimulus.source_note: Data table from the United States federal census, 1790-1840: free and enslaved Black population. Totals checked against the Census Bureau's Negro Population 1790-1915 and Gannett, Statistics of the Negroes in the United States (1894).

source: original; data table from the United States federal census, 1790-1840
stem: The enslaved population kept growing after Congress banned importation in 1808. What best explains that growth?

options.text: Large numbers of enslaved people kept arriving from Africa after 1808
options.misconception: Importation was banned; smuggling was small beside the growth shown.

options.text: Northern states freed their slaves and sent them south
options.misconception: Northern emancipation freed people in the North; it did not grow the enslaved South.

options.text: The census stopped counting enslaved children after 1808
options.misconception: Children born to enslaved mothers were counted as enslaved.

options.text: Children born into slavery, and the domestic trade moving enslaved people south

rationales.A: The ban closed the legal trade from Africa. The growth after 1808 came from inside the country, not from new arrivals.
rationales.B: Northern states freed enslaved people slowly, and those people stayed free in the North. They were not sent south as slaves.
rationales.C: The census counted enslaved children. Children born to enslaved mothers were born enslaved.
rationales.D: Enslaved families grew by birth, and traders moved enslaved people from the Upper South to the cotton South.
rationales.general:
1. Rule out imports. Congress banned importation from abroad, effective 1808.
2. Ask where growth could come from inside the country. Children born to enslaved mothers were born enslaved.
3. Ask why the South needed more workers. Cotton growers bought enslaved people and moved them south.
Background: Historians estimate about one million enslaved people were moved south in the domestic trade between 1808 and 1865.
Remember: when a door closes, ask which other doors stayed open.
